opus-5.5.text:
When I first joined, I didn't think of it as two completely different schools. Everyone was working from roughly the same toolbox: pretrain a strong base model, then use some combination of supervised fine-tuning, preference learning, and reinforcement learning to shape it. The differences I noticed were more about emphasis and taste than about secret algorithms.

From the outside, OpenAI seemed to lean into scaling RL as a capability engine. The reasoning-model line made that very visible: if you have tasks with verifiable rewards, like math, code, or anything you can check, and you let the model think longer and optimize hard against those signals, capabilities keep improving. The bet was that RL isn't just polishing, it's another axis you can scale.

At Anthropic, my first impression was that people treated post-training as being as much about the model's character and judgment as about raw capability. There was a lot of attention on how the model behaves: is it honest, does it know when it's uncertain, does it act sensibly in long agentic tasks without doing something weird to hit the reward. Constitution-style approaches came out of that, using principles and model feedback instead of relying only on human labels. And I found the culture quite empirical and careful about reward hacking. When the model gets better at the metric, people ask whether it actually got better at the thing you care about.

Over time I came to think the two views are converging. Everyone now agrees RL at scale matters a lot, and everyone also realizes that once models become agents doing real work, the reward signal is the hard part. Coding is a good example. It looks verifiable, but "passes the tests" and "is good software a person would want" aren't the same. So the interesting question is less "who does RL better" and more "who builds the environments and rewards that actually capture what we want." I think that's where a lot of the real differentiation is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he did not see the approaches as two completely different schools and describes their differences as emphasis and taste, so it does not communicate that he viewed them as substantially different when he joined.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get a lot, and I should say upfront that most of what I can talk about is the public picture plus my own framing, not internal details from either place.

When I joined, my honest first impression was that the two labs are much more similar than the outside narrative suggests. At the level of the core recipe, everyone is doing roughly the same thing: you take a strong pretrained model, you build environments where the model has to act and get feedback, you define rewards, and you run RL at scale. The algorithms are not the secret. The differences live in three places: what you choose to optimize for, how you build and prioritize environments, and what you believe about where the generalization comes from.

On the first one, my sense of OpenAI's culture was that reasoning was treated as the main axis. Make the model think longer, think better, and a lot of capabilities fall out downstream. Anthropic, at least as I perceived it, puts more weight on the model as an agent operating over a long horizon, especially in coding. Reasoning matters, but it is one ingredient in a bigger loop of planning, tool use, recovering from mistakes, and staying coherent across many steps. Those are not contradictory views, but they do pull resource allocation and evaluation design in different directions.

The second difference is about environments, and this is where I spent a lot of my own career, with things like SWE-bench and tau-bench. In the second half of AI, as I like to put it, the bottleneck is less about new methods and more about defining the right problems. What tasks do you build? How realistic is the feedback? How do you avoid the model learning to game your grader? Both labs understand this, but the taste in which environments are worth the enormous cost of building is where you really see the philosophy. Anthropic's taste skews toward tasks that look like real work people actually delegate.

The third thing, and probably the most interesting to me intellectually, is the question of priors. RL only works when the pretrained model already has a prior that puts the right behaviors within reach. Language gives you that prior. So part of the job is figuring out what to put into the model before RL so that RL has something to shape. I found Anthropic very thoughtful about the interplay between the character of the model, its alignment behavior, and its capabilities, rather than treating safety as a separate stage you bolt on at the end. That changes how you design the reward too.

So if you ask me to summarize, I would say the methods converged, the evaluations diverged, and the real competition is in taste about what problems matter. That was actually a big part of why I made the move. I wanted to be somewhere that treated building the right environments as a first-class research problem instead of as infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response says the labs were “much more similar” and their core RL recipe and methods had converged. It describes differences in priorities and environments, but does not characterize their overall approaches as substantially different.

astra-6.text:
The way I’d frame the difference is to ask what reinforcement learning is supposed to accomplish in post-training. One role is alignment: taking a pretrained model and making its behavior more helpful, reliable, and consistent with what people want. Another role is capability development: using feedback to teach the model to solve problems it couldn’t solve before.

Those roles overlap, so I wouldn’t draw a clean line where Anthropic represents one and OpenAI represents the other. The interesting question is where you put the emphasis, and what kinds of feedback you can scale. If you can verify an answer, as in some coding or math tasks, you have a relatively clear training signal. For more open-ended tasks, specifying what counts as success becomes much harder.

I’d also distinguish that conceptual understanding from knowing the internal recipes. You can have a useful picture of the research direction without knowing exactly how either company’s training system works.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different roles for reinforcement learning and possible differences in emphasis, but does not say that Shunyu Yao saw Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s approaches as substantially different when he joined Anthropic. It instead cautions against assigning each company a distinct role.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish the technical approach from the philosophy behind it. Both were using reinforcement learning to improve a pretrained model through feedback. The interesting questions were: Where does that feedback come from, what behavior does it reward, and how well does that reward capture what we actually want?

Anthropic’s public work put a lot of emphasis on Constitutional AI—using explicit principles to guide feedback, including feedback generated by another model. OpenAI’s public work emphasized learning from human preferences. But that’s a difference in emphasis, not a clean separation between two completely different methods.

I’d also be careful about inferring an organization’s whole approach from those labels. For me, the deeper question is whether post-training is teaching the model to produce answers that people prefer, or helping it solve problems it couldn’t solve before. Those objectives overlap, but they aren’t identical, and the reward signal matters enormously.

r001.rationale: The response describes a difference in emphasis between the organizations, but explicitly says it was not a clean separation between different methods. It does not state that Yao saw their approaches as substantially different when he joined Anthropic.
